topics.title: The Preamble and the basic structure doctrine
topics.hook: The Preamble is the Constitution stating its own purpose, and the basic structure doctrine is the Supreme Court deciding that purpose cannot be amended away.
topics.story:
The Preamble was adopted on 26 November 1949 and reads that "We, the People of India" resolve to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic. Three of those words were not there originally. The 42nd Amendment of 1976, passed during the Emergency, inserted **socialist**, **secular** and **integrity**. That single fact accounts for a large share of Preamble questions.

The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, but the Preamble's own date is 26 November 1949, which is why that day is Constitution Day. The date in the Preamble is the date of adoption, not commencement, and papers exploit the gap.

Whether the Preamble is part of the Constitution took two cases to settle. In *Berubari Union* (1960) the Court said it was not. In *Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala* (1973) it reversed itself: the Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended, but not so as to destroy the basic features it declares.

Kesavananda is the most important judgment in Indian constitutional law. A bench of thirteen judges, still the largest ever assembled, held by 7-6 that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is wide but not unlimited. It cannot alter the basic structure. The Court has never given a closed list of what that structure contains, which is deliberate: supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections and the independence of the judiciary have all been held to be part of it in later cases.

The doctrine has teeth. *Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain* (1975) struck down a constitutional amendment for the first time. *Minerva Mills* (1980) struck down clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368, which had tried to make amendments immune from review. *S.R. Bommai* (1994) applied it to secularism. *I.R. Coelho* (2007) held that even laws parked in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda, are open to review if they damage the basic structure.

The objectives in the Preamble read as a set: justice (social, economic, political), liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), equality (of status and opportunity), and fraternity (assuring dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation). The ordering is worth memorising because questions are built on it.

facts.k: First case to hold Preamble not part of Constitution
First amendment struck down for violating basic structure

topics.title: Fundamental Rights: Part III, Articles 12 to 35
topics.hook: Six rights, one definition clause, one clause that voids inconsistent laws, and a remedy the Constitution itself calls its heart.
topics.story:
Part III runs from Article 12 to Article 35. It originally contained seven Fundamental Rights. The right to property, Article 31, was removed by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and re-planted as an ordinary legal right in Article 300A. Six remain:

- Right to Equality, Articles 14 to 18
- Right to Freedom, Articles 19 to 22
- Right against Exploitation, Articles 23 and 24
- Right to Freedom of Religion, Articles 25 to 28
- Cultural and Educational Rights, Articles 29 and 30
- Right to Constitutional Remedies, Article 32

Article 12 defines "the State" for the whole of Part III: the Government and Parliament of India, the government and legislature of each state, all local authorities and "other authorities" within India or under the control of the Government of India. That last phrase is the litigated one. Courts have brought statutory corporations, and in some cases private bodies discharging public functions, within its net. Fundamental Rights are ordinarily enforceable against the State, not against private persons, with the exceptions of Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24, which bind everyone.

Article 13 does the enforcing. Pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Part III are void to the extent of the inconsistency, and the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges these rights. Article 13(2) is where judicial review of legislation formally lives. Article 13(3) defines "law" widely enough to include ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, custom and usage.

Two doctrines come straight out of Article 13. **Eclipse**: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but dormant, and revives if the inconsistency is removed. **Severability**: only the offending part is struck down if it can be separated from the rest.

Articles 33 to 35 close Part III. Article 33 lets Parliament restrict these rights for the armed forces and police. Article 34 allows restriction while martial law is in force. Article 35 reserves to Parliament alone the power to legislate on certain Part III matters.

Fundamental Rights are not absolute. Every one of them carries reasonable restrictions written into the text, and under Article 359 their enforcement, other than Articles 20 and 21, can be suspended during a National Emergency. Articles 20 and 21 became non-suspendable through the 44th Amendment, a direct answer to *ADM Jabalpur* (1976), where the Court had held that even the right to life could be suspended. That judgment was formally repudiated in *Puttaswamy* (2017).

facts.v: Right to Property, Article 31, by the 44th Amendment, 1978

facts.k: Cannot be suspended in an Emergency

facts.v: The United States Bill of Rights

topics.why: The most common trap is the count: six rights, not seven, and property is the one that left. Expect a passage on a rights dispute to test Article 12 or Article 13 rather than the headline right itself.

topics.title: Article 21: how one sentence became the whole of Indian rights law
topics.hook: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Twenty-two words that now carry privacy, a clean environment, education, livelihood and the right to die with dignity.
topics.story:
The drafters deliberately wrote **procedure established by law**, a Japanese formulation, rather than the American **due process of law**. B.N. Rau had met Justice Felix Frankfurter, who warned that due process gave judges too much power. The choice mattered immediately.

In *A.K. Gopalan* (1950) the Supreme Court read the phrase literally: if a law laid down a procedure, that was enough, and Articles 19, 21 and 22 were watertight compartments. The result was that preventive detention survived almost any challenge.

*Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India* (1978) demolished that reading. Maneka Gandhi's passport had been impounded without reasons. A seven-judge bench held that the procedure must be **right, just and fair**, not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive, and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are to be read together as a golden triangle. Due process entered the Constitution through the back door and has never left.

Everything after 1978 is expansion. Article 21 has been held to include the right to live with human dignity (*Francis Coralie Mullin*, 1981), livelihood (*Olga Tellis*, 1985), a clean environment (*Subhash Kumar*, 1991, and the M.C. Mehta line of cases), health, shelter, legal aid, a speedy trial, privacy (*Puttaswamy*, 2017), and the right to die with dignity through a passive euthanasia framework and living wills (*Common Cause*, 2018). Education was read in through *Unni Krishnan* (1993) and then written in as Article 21A by the 86th Amendment in 2002, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged six to fourteen, implemented by the Right to Education Act 2009.

*Puttaswamy* is the anchor of the modern law. Nine judges held unanimously that privacy is a Fundamental Right under Article 21. It overruled *M.P. Sharma* (1954) and *Kharak Singh* (1962) on the point, laid down a proportionality test for state intrusion, and expressly repudiated *ADM Jabalpur*. The judgment led to the Aadhaar verdict of 2018 and to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023.

Article 21 protects **any person**, citizen or not, and along with Article 20 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency, a change made by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

facts.v: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law"
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002; ages 6 to 14
Common Cause v. Union of India, 2018

facts.k: Cannot be suspended in an Emergency

timeline.what: Maneka Gandhi: procedure must be right, just and fair
Common Cause: right to die with dignity

topics.why: Any passage on surveillance, data, environment, housing, health or euthanasia is an Article 21 question. Examiners love the "procedure established by law" versus "due process" contrast and the country each came from.

topics.title: Article 32, Article 226 and the five writs
topics.hook: Five Latin names, two articles, and one distinction the exam asks about every year: the Supreme Court writ is a Fundamental Right, the High Court writ is wider.
topics.story:
Article 32 gives every person the right to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and empowers the Court to issue directions, orders or writs. It is itself a Fundamental Right, which is why Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution, and why it cannot be suspended except under Article 359 during an emergency.

Article 226 gives High Courts the same writ power. The two differ in two ways that matter. Article 32 is available **only** for Fundamental Rights; Article 226 is available for Fundamental Rights **and for any other legal right**, so it is territorially and substantively wider. And Article 32 is a right, so the Supreme Court cannot refuse to entertain a petition; Article 226 is a discretionary power, so a High Court may decline.

The five writs come from English law:

- **Habeas corpus**, "you may have the body". Against unlawful detention. Issued against both public authorities and private persons.
- **Mandamus**, "we command". Orders a public authority to perform a public duty. Not available against a private individual, the President or Governors, or to enforce a purely discretionary or contractual duty.
- **Prohibition**, issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to stop it exceeding its jurisdiction. Preventive, issued while proceedings are pending, and only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
- **Certiorari**, "to be certified". Quashes an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal. Curative rather than preventive. Since *Surya Dev Rai* (2003) it also runs against administrative bodies affecting rights.
- **Quo warranto**, "by what authority". Questions the legality of a person's claim to a public office. Any interested person may seek it, not just the aggrieved party.

Public interest litigation grew out of Article 32 in the late 1970s and 1980s, associated above all with Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer. It relaxed *locus standi* so that any public-spirited person could move the Court on behalf of those unable to do so, and treated letters and postcards as petitions. *Hussainara Khatoon* (1979), on undertrials in Bihar, is usually cited as the first true PIL.

facts.v: Right to constitutional remedies, a Fundamental Right in itself
High Court writ jurisdiction, wider in scope

facts.k: Writ questioning a public office holder
Called the heart and soul of the Constitution

facts.v: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, 1979

topics.why: A passage about someone detained, or an official appointed without qualification, is testing which writ applies. Learn the pairs: certiorari quashes, prohibition prevents; mandamus commands a duty, quo warranto challenges an office.

topics.title: Article 14 and the two tests of equality
topics.hook: Equality before the law is British, equal protection of the laws is American, and Indian courts read the same article two different ways depending on which test they reach for.
topics.story:
Article 14 says the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. Two phrases, two sources. **Equality before the law** is a negative concept borrowed from the British rule of law as stated by A.V. Dicey: no one is above the law. **Equal protection of the laws** is positive and taken from the Fourteenth Amendment of the US Constitution: like should be treated alike.

Note "any person", not "any citizen". Article 14 protects foreigners and corporations too. Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29 are limited to citizens; 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25 to 28 are available to all persons.

Equality does not mean uniformity. The classical test, from *State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar* (1952) and refined since, allows the State to classify if two conditions are met: the classification rests on an **intelligible differentia**, and that differentia has a **rational nexus** with the object the law seeks to achieve. A law taxing incomes above a threshold classifies, and lawfully so.

*E.P. Royappa* (1974) opened a second route. Justice Bhagwati wrote that equality is antithetical to arbitrariness, so any arbitrary State action violates Article 14 without needing a comparator at all. *Maneka Gandhi* (1978) cemented it, and the arbitrariness test is now the one courts reach for most often. *Shayara Bano* (2017) used it to strike down instant triple talaq.

Exceptions written into the Constitution matter for questions. The President and Governors enjoy immunity under Article 361: no criminal proceedings during the term of office and no civil proceedings without two months' notice. Article 105 and Article 194 protect members of Parliament and state legislatures for anything said or any vote given in the House. Foreign diplomats and UN bodies have immunity under international law.

facts.v: Any person, including foreigners and companies

topics.why: Passages on reservation, on a new tax, or on any rule that treats one group differently are Article 14 questions. The examiner usually wants the two-limb classification test named correctly, or the "person versus citizen" distinction.

nodes.label: Article 14
nodes.note: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws." Applies to persons, not only citizens.

nodes.label: Reasonable classification
nodes.note: Two limbs: intelligible differentia, and a rational nexus between that differentia and the object of the law. From Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952).

nodes.label: E.P. Royappa (1974)
nodes.note: Justice P.N. Bhagwati held equality is antithetical to arbitrariness. Arbitrary State action breaches Article 14 on its own.

nodes.label: A.V. Dicey

nodes.label: Maneka Gandhi (1978)

topics.title: Emergency provisions: Articles 352, 356 and 360
topics.hook: Three kinds of emergency, one of which has been used more than a hundred times and one of which has never been used at all.
topics.story:
Part XVIII contains three emergencies, borrowed in structure from the Government of India Act 1935 and the Weimar Constitution.

**National Emergency, Article 352.** Declared on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The original text said "internal disturbance"; the 44th Amendment of 1978 replaced it with "armed rebellion", precisely because the vague earlier phrase had been used in 1975. A proclamation now needs the written recommendation of the Cabinet, must be approved by both Houses by a special majority within one month, and lasts six months at a time. During it, Article 19 freedoms are suspended under Article 358 (only for a war or external aggression emergency, after 1978), and the enforcement of other Part III rights can be suspended under Article 359, except Articles 20 and 21. It has been declared three times: 1962 (China), 1971 (Pakistan) and 1975 (internal disturbance).

**President's Rule, Article 356.** Imposed when the President is satisfied that the government of a state cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, usually on the Governor's report. Approval by both Houses by simple majority within two months, then six months at a time, to a maximum of three years. It has been used well over a hundred times, most aggressively in the 1970s and 1980s. *S.R. Bommai v. Union of India* (1994) changed that: a nine-judge bench held the proclamation is subject to judicial review, that the floor of the House and not the Governor's opinion is the test of majority, and that a dissolved assembly can be revived if the proclamation is struck down. Article 365 is the companion provision: failure to comply with a Union direction can itself trigger 356.

**Financial Emergency, Article 360.** Declared if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has never been declared. During it the Union may direct states on money bills and reduce the salaries of all officials including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

The 44th Amendment, passed by the Janata government after the 1977 election, is the single most important reform here. It raised the threshold for a national emergency, required a written Cabinet recommendation, made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable, restored judicial review, and cut the Lok Sabha's term back to five years from the six that the 42nd Amendment had set.

facts.v: Government of India Act 1935 and the Weimar Constitution

topics.why: Any passage on a state government falling, a Governor’s report, or a hung assembly is an Article 356 question, and Bommai is the case they want named. The classic trap is asking which emergency has never been proclaimed.

topics.title: Parliament: two Houses, and the money bill that only one of them controls
topics.hook: The Lok Sabha can be dissolved and the Rajya Sabha cannot, the Rajya Sabha can only delay a money bill by fourteen days, and the Speaker decides what a money bill is.
topics.story:
Parliament under Article 79 consists of the President and two Houses. The President is part of Parliament, which is a favourite one-mark point.

**Lok Sabha.** Maximum strength 550 under Article 81: up to 530 from states and 20 from Union Territories. The two Anglo-Indian nominated seats under Article 331 were discontinued by the 104th Amendment in 2020. Present strength is 543. Term is five years, extendable by one year at a time during a national emergency. It can be dissolved.

**Rajya Sabha.** Maximum 250 under Article 80: up to 238 elected by state and UT legislatures and 12 nominated by the President for literature, science, art and social service. Present strength is 245. It is a permanent body, never dissolved, with one third retiring every two years, so a member's term is six years. Its representation is not equal by state, unlike the American Senate; it follows population, which is why Uttar Pradesh has 31 seats and Sikkim has one.

**Money bills, Article 110.** A bill dealing only with taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund. Three consequences follow. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha must return it within fourteen days and can only recommend, not amend. And the Speaker's certificate that a bill is a money bill is final. That last point produced serious litigation over the Aadhaar Act and the Finance Act 2017, both passed as money bills.

A **financial bill** is broader and does not carry all these protections; the distinction is a standard question. There is no joint sitting for a money bill, because there can be no deadlock. Joint sittings under Article 108 are for ordinary bills and have happened three times: the Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, the Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill 1978, and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill 2002.

Sessions: Budget, Monsoon and Winter. The maximum gap between two sessions is six months. Adjournment ends a sitting, prorogation ends a session, dissolution ends the House itself. A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha and needs the support of at least 50 members to be admitted.

facts.v: The President and two Houses, Article 79
Six years, one third retiring every two years
Article 110; Rajya Sabha has 14 days and can only recommend
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha, and the certificate is final

topics.why: Passages on a contested bill almost always turn on the money bill route, because that is how a government bypasses the Rajya Sabha. Know the 14 days, the Speaker’s certificate, and that no joint sitting is possible.

topics.title: The judiciary: appointments, the collegium and the NJAC that never was
topics.hook: Judges appointing judges is not in the Constitution. It is the result of three cases, and Parliament’s attempt to undo it lasted eleven months.
topics.story:
Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court and says judges are appointed by the President after consultation with such judges as the President thinks fit. The plain text gives the executive the upper hand. Three judgments turned it round.

**First Judges Case**, *S.P. Gupta* (1981): "consultation" does not mean "concurrence", so the executive had primacy. **Second Judges Case**, *Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association* (1993): consultation does mean concurrence, and the CJI's view has primacy. **Third Judges Case** (1998), an advisory opinion under Article 143 on a Presidential reference: the CJI must act through a collegium of the four senior-most judges, five in all. That is the collegium, and it exists nowhere in the constitutional text.

Parliament tried to replace it. The 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, both of 2014, created a six-member NJAC: the CJI, the two next senior judges, the Law Minister and two eminent persons. In *Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India* (2015), a five-judge bench struck both down 4-1, holding that judicial independence and the primacy of the judiciary in appointments are part of the basic structure. Justice J. Chelameswar dissented.

The numbers. The Supreme Court's sanctioned strength is 34 including the Chief Justice, set by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act 2019. A judge retires at 65; a High Court judge at 62. Removal, under Article 124(4), is by an address of both Houses supported by a majority of the total membership and two thirds of those present and voting, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The Constitution never uses the word impeachment for judges. No judge has ever been removed; Justice V. Ramaswami survived in 1993 when the Congress abstained.

Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts. Article 142 lets it pass any order necessary for complete justice, the provision used in the Ayodhya and Bhopal settlements. Article 143 is the advisory jurisdiction. Article 137 allows review and Article 145 the constitution of benches; the curative petition, a further step after review, was invented in *Rupa Ashok Hurra* (2002).

topics.title: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
topics.hook: Non-justiciable instructions to the State, borrowed from Ireland, that courts have used anyway to decide what Article 21 means.
topics.story:
Part IV, Articles 36 to 51, holds the Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 37 makes the position explicit: they are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. India took the idea from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which took it from Spain.

They sort into three families, though the Constitution does not label them. **Socialist**: Article 38 (welfare state), Article 39 (adequate means of livelihood, distribution of material resources to subserve the common good, equal pay for equal work, no abuse of children), Article 39A (free legal aid), Article 41 (right to work, education, public assistance), Article 42 (maternity relief), Article 43 (living wage), Article 43A (workers' participation in management). **Gandhian**: Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 43B (co-operative societies), Article 46 (SC and ST interests), Article 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks), Article 48 (prohibition of cow slaughter). **Liberal-intellectual**: Article 44 (uniform civil code), Article 45 (early childhood care), Article 48A (environment and forests), Article 49 (monuments), Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), Article 51 (international peace).

The relationship with Fundamental Rights was fought over for thirty years. *Champakam Dorairajan* (1951) held rights prevail. Article 31C, added in 1971, gave certain Directive Principles precedence. *Minerva Mills* (1980) settled it: the balance between Parts III and IV is itself part of the basic structure, so neither can swallow the other.

**Fundamental Duties** live in Part IVA, Article 51A, and were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. There were ten; the 86th Amendment in 2002 added an eleventh, the duty of a parent or guardian to provide education to a child aged six to fourteen. They are borrowed from the Soviet constitution and are, like the Directive Principles, non-justiciable.

topics.why: Passages on welfare schemes, the uniform civil code or environmental regulation lean on Part IV. The reliable question is which article carries which principle, and that duties are non-justiciable.

topics.title: Constitutional, statutory and executive bodies: the distinction they always test
topics.hook: The Election Commission is constitutional, the NHRC is statutory, and NITI Aayog is neither. Getting that sorting right is worth more marks than knowing what any of them do.
topics.story:
A **constitutional body** is created by the Constitution itself and named in an article. A **statutory body** is created by an Act of Parliament. An **executive** or **non-statutory** body is created by a government resolution and can be wound up the same way.

Constitutional bodies and their articles: Election Commission (324), Union and State Public Service Commissions (315), Finance Commission (280), Comptroller and Auditor General (148), Attorney General (76), Advocate General (165), National Commission for Scheduled Castes (338), for Scheduled Tribes (338A), for Backward Classes (338B, added by the 102nd Amendment in 2018), Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (350B), Inter-State Council (263), GST Council (279A, added by the 101st Amendment in 2016).

Statutory bodies: National Human Rights Commission (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993), Central Information Commission (RTI Act 2005), Central Vigilance Commission (CVC Act 2003, after *Vineet Narain*), Lokpal (Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013), National Commission for Women (1990), NGT (National Green Tribunal Act 2010), SEBI (1992), TRAI, NCPCR, and the RBI (Reserve Bank of India Act 1934).

Executive bodies: NITI Aayog, set up by a Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015 to replace the Planning Commission, which was itself a 1950 executive body. The Central Bureau of Investigation is an unusual case: it functions under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946, so it is statutory in derivation though not created as a standalone body.

Two details recur. The CAG under Article 148 is appointed by the President for six years or until 65, removable only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge, and Ambedkar called the office the most important in the Constitution. The Election Commission became a three-member body permanently in 1993; the Chief Election Commissioner is removable like a Supreme Court judge, while the other two commissioners are removable on the CEC's recommendation, which is why the Court and Parliament have fought over the appointment process.

Article 280, constitutional; constituted every five years

topics.why: The question is almost never what a body does. It is whether the body is constitutional or statutory, and which article or Act created it. Learn the sorting first and the functions second.

topics.title: Federalism and the Seventh Schedule
topics.hook: Three lists, one residuary power, and a Constitution that calls itself a Union of States rather than a federation.
topics.story:
Article 1 says India, that is Bharat, shall be a **Union of States**. Ambedkar explained the wording: the Union is indestructible, and the states derive their existence from it rather than from any agreement to join. That is why Article 3 lets Parliament create, rename or redraw states by simple majority, with the state legislature only entitled to express a view that Parliament may ignore.

The **Seventh Schedule** divides subjects under Article 246. The **Union List** has 97 entries as originally drafted, including defence, foreign affairs, railways, banking, currency, atomic energy and citizenship. The **State List** has 66, including public order, police, public health, agriculture, land and local government. The **Concurrent List** has 47, including criminal law and procedure, marriage and divorce, contracts, bankruptcy, education and forests. Education and forests were moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

Where a Union law and a state law on a Concurrent subject conflict, Article 254 makes the Union law prevail, unless the state law received Presidential assent, in which case it operates in that state. Residuary powers, under Article 248 and entry 97 of the Union List, belong to Parliament, unlike in the United States where they rest with the states.

Parliament can legislate on a State List subject in five situations: a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 passed by two thirds, a national emergency under Article 250, a request by two or more states under Article 252, to implement an international treaty under Article 253, and during President's Rule.

Interpretation doctrines: **pith and substance** looks at the true character of a law rather than incidental encroachment, **colourable legislation** strikes down a law doing indirectly what the legislature cannot do directly, and **repugnancy** is the Article 254 conflict rule. Commissions on centre-state relations: Sarkaria (1983), Punchhi (2007), and the Rajamannar Committee before them.

facts.v: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States

topics.title: The President: election, powers and the ordinance route
topics.hook: Elected by an electoral college that includes no ordinary voter, bound by ministerial advice since 1976, and able to legislate for six weeks at a time when Parliament is not sitting.
topics.story:
Article 52 creates the office. The President is elected under Article 54 by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the legislative assemblies of the states, plus Delhi and Puducherry. Nominated members do not vote. The election is by proportional representation with a single transferable vote and a secret ballot, under Article 55, and the value of each vote is weighted by population using the 1971 census, frozen there by the 84th Amendment.

Qualifications under Article 58: citizen of India, at least 35, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha, and not holding an office of profit. The term is five years, re-election is permitted without limit, and removal is by **impeachment** under Article 61 for violation of the Constitution, the only impeachment the Constitution provides for. The charge may originate in either House, needs a resolution signed by a quarter of the members with fourteen days' notice, and must pass both Houses by two thirds of total membership. Nominated members do vote in an impeachment, though they cannot vote in the election.

Article 74 requires the President to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The 42nd Amendment made this binding in terms; the 44th Amendment added that the President may return advice once for reconsideration, after which the advice is binding.

Legislative powers matter most for the exam. Under Article 111 the President may assent to a bill, withhold assent, or return a non-money bill for reconsideration; if the Houses pass it again, assent must be given. There is no time limit, which produces the so-called **pocket veto**, famously used by President Zail Singh on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986. Under Article 123 the President may promulgate an **ordinance** when either House is not in session; it has the same force as an Act, must be laid before Parliament, and ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles. *D.C. Wadhwa* (1987) condemned the re-promulgation of ordinances in Bihar, and *Krishna Kumar Singh* (2017) held that repeated re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution.

topics.title: Amending the Constitution, and the amendments worth knowing by number
topics.hook: Three procedures, one of which is not even in Article 368, and about a dozen amendment numbers that carry most of the marks.
topics.story:
Article 368 provides the amendment procedure, borrowed in spirit from South Africa. There are three routes.

**Simple majority.** Some provisions are amended like ordinary law and are outside Article 368 altogether: creating or abolishing states under Article 3, changing state boundaries or names, creating or abolishing legislative councils under Article 169, citizenship provisions, and Schedules 5 and 6 in part.

**Special majority.** Most of the Constitution. A majority of the total membership of each House plus two thirds of members present and voting. Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles go this way.

**Special majority plus state ratification.** Provisions affecting the federal structure: the election of the President, the extent of executive power of the Union and states, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the distribution of legislative powers, the Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself. Ratification by the legislatures of at least half the states is needed, by simple majority, and there is no time limit.

Amendments worth memorising: **1st (1951)** added Ninth Schedule and Article 15(4). **7th (1956)** reorganised states after the States Reorganisation Act. **42nd (1976)** the "mini-Constitution", added Socialist, Secular, Integrity, Fundamental Duties and Part IVA, extended the Lok Sabha term. **44th (1978)** reversed much of it and removed the right to property. **52nd (1985)** anti-defection, Tenth Schedule. **61st (1988)** voting age lowered from 21 to 18. **73rd and 74th (1992)** panchayats and municipalities, Schedules 11 and 12. **86th (2002)** Article 21A. **91st (2003)** capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength. **97th (2011)** co-operative societies. **101st (2016)** GST. **102nd (2018)** constitutional status for the NCBC. **103rd (2019)** 10% EWS reservation, upheld 3-2 in *Janhit Abhiyan* (2022). **104th (2020)** ended Anglo-Indian nomination, extended SC and ST reservation in legislatures. **106th (2023)** Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserving one third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after a delimitation following the next census.

topics.title: Making the Constitution, and what was borrowed from where
topics.hook: Two years, eleven months and eighteen days, 389 members at the start, and a document that openly took its best ideas from eight other countries.
topics.story:
The Constituent Assembly was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 and first met on **9 December 1946**. Sachchidananda Sinha was interim chairman as the oldest member; **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. After Partition the strength fell to 299.

**Jawaharlal Nehru** moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947, which became the Preamble in condensed form. The **Drafting Committee** was constituted on 29 August 1947 with **B.R. Ambedkar** as chairman and six other members. **B.N. Rau** was the Constitutional Adviser, and it was Rau's draft the committee worked from.

The Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** and came into force on **26 January 1950**, a date chosen because the Congress had declared Purna Swaraj on 26 January 1930. Total time taken: 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. The original text had **395 articles, 22 parts and 8 schedules**; it now runs to about 470 articles, 25 parts and 12 schedules.

Borrowed features, the single most reliably asked table:

- **Britain**: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, the Speaker, legislative procedure, prerogative writs, cabinet system, bicameralism
- **United States**: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of the judiciary, impeachment of the President, removal of judges, the office of Vice President, preamble wording
- **Ireland**: Directive Principles, method of electing the President, nomination to the Rajya Sabha
- **Canada**: federation with a strong centre, the word Union, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
- **Australia**: Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, joint sitting of the two Houses
- **Germany, Weimar**: suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency
- **USSR**: Fundamental Duties, the ideal of justice in the Preamble
- **France**: liberty, equality and fraternity; the republic
- **South Africa**: amendment procedure, election of Rajya Sabha members
- **Japan**: procedure established by law

The **twelve schedules**: 1 states and UTs, 2 emoluments, 3 forms of oath, 4 Rajya Sabha seat allocation, 5 scheduled areas, 6 tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, 7 the three lists, 8 the 22 languages, 9 protected laws, 10 anti-defection, 11 panchayat subjects, 12 municipal subjects.
topics.why: The borrowed-features table and the schedule list are pure recall and appear almost every year. The classic trap pairs Directive Principles with the wrong country: they came from Ireland, not Britain.

topics.title: Anti-defection and the Tenth Schedule
topics.hook: A law meant to stop horse-trading that now turns on how fast a Speaker chooses to decide.
topics.story:
The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the **52nd Amendment in 1985** under Rajiv Gandhi, after a decade in which the phrase "Aaya Ram Gaya Ram" had become shorthand for legislators changing sides. It disqualifies a member of Parliament or a state legislature on two grounds: **voluntarily giving up membership** of the party on whose ticket they were elected, and **voting or abstaining contrary to a party whip** without prior permission and without being condoned within fifteen days.

"Voluntarily giving up membership" is wider than resignation. Courts have read conduct, public statements and attendance at a rival party's events as enough.

The original schedule allowed a **split**: if one third of a legislature party broke away, they were protected. That exemption was deleted by the **91st Amendment in 2003**, which also capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House and barred a disqualified member from holding a ministerial post for the rest of the term. What survives is **merger**, which requires two thirds of the legislature party to agree.

The presiding officer decides. That is the design flaw. In *Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu* (1992) the Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule but struck down paragraph 7, which had tried to bar judicial review, holding that the Speaker acts as a tribunal and the decision is reviewable, though only after it is made. Because there is no time limit, a Speaker who wants a particular outcome can simply not decide. *Keisham Meghachandra Singh* (2020) recommended deciding within three months and suggested Parliament consider moving the power to an independent tribunal. Nothing has changed.

The nominated member rule is a common question: a nominated member of a House may join a political party within six months of taking a seat without attracting disqualification, and is disqualified if they join one after that.

topics.title: Local government: the 73rd and 74th Amendments
topics.hook: Constitutional status for the third tier, a fixed five-year term, and a third of all seats reserved for women.
topics.story:
Article 40, a Directive Principle, asked the State to organise village panchayats. It took forty-two years and two amendments to make that binding.

The **73rd Amendment (1992)** added **Part IX**, Articles 243 to 243O, and the **Eleventh Schedule** with 29 subjects. It provides a three-tier structure in states with a population above twenty lakh: **gram panchayat** at village level, **panchayat samiti** at block level and **zila parishad** at district level. Every panchayat has a five-year term, and elections must be held before it expires or within six months of dissolution. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to population, and **not less than one third** of all seats and chairperson posts are reserved for women. A **State Election Commission** conducts the polls and a **State Finance Commission** is constituted every five years under Article 243-I. The **gram sabha**, the body of all registered voters in a village, is the foundation; Article 243A leaves its powers to state law.

The **74th Amendment (1992)** did the same for urban areas: **Part IXA**, Articles 243P to 243ZG, and the **Twelfth Schedule** with 18 subjects. Three kinds of municipality: **nagar panchayat** for an area in transition from rural to urban, **municipal council** for a smaller urban area, and **municipal corporation** for a larger one. Ward committees are mandatory in municipalities with more than three lakh people. Both amendments came into force in 1993.

Neither amendment devolves anything by itself. The Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules are lists of subjects that state legislatures **may** entrust, and the extent of actual devolution of funds, functions and functionaries varies enormously between states. Kerala and Karnataka devolve heavily; several states have kept most powers.

Earlier committees run in a line: **Balwant Rai Mehta (1957)** recommended the three-tier system and democratic decentralisation, Rajasthan being the first state to adopt it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. **Ashok Mehta (1977)** recommended a two-tier system. **L.M. Singhvi (1986)** first recommended constitutional status.

facts.k: First state to adopt panchayati raj

topics.why: Expect a passage on rural governance or municipal finance. The two numbers that decide the question are the schedule count, 29 and 18, and the one-third women’s reservation.

topics.title: Citizenship: Articles 5 to 11 and the Citizenship Act
topics.hook: The Constitution deals only with who was a citizen in 1950. Everything since is ordinary law, which is why citizenship can be changed without amending the Constitution.
topics.story:
**Articles 5 to 11** in Part II settle citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. Article 5 covers those domiciled in India, Article 6 migrants from Pakistan, Article 7 those who migrated to Pakistan and returned, Article 8 persons of Indian origin abroad, Article 9 says a person voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship is not an Indian citizen, Article 10 provides for continuance, and **Article 11 gives Parliament full power to legislate on citizenship**. That last article is why the Citizenship Act can be amended by ordinary majority.

The **Citizenship Act 1955** provides five ways to acquire citizenship: by **birth**, by **descent**, by **registration**, by **naturalisation**, and by **incorporation of territory**. The birth rule has been tightened twice. Anyone born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987 is a citizen by birth regardless of parentage. Between 1 July 1987 and 3 December 2004, one parent must have been a citizen. On or after 3 December 2004, one parent must be a citizen and the other must not be an illegal migrant.

India allows only **single citizenship**, a British inheritance, unlike the United States where a person is a citizen of both the country and a state. There is no dual citizenship; the **Overseas Citizen of India** card, created in 2005, is a long-term visa and confers no voting rights, no public office and no agricultural land purchase.

The **Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019** made non-Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 eligible for citizenship on a shortened naturalisation period. It excludes Muslims, which is the basis of the challenge under Article 14 still pending before the Supreme Court, and it does not apply to Sixth Schedule tribal areas or Inner Line Permit states. Citizenship can be lost by renunciation, termination on acquiring foreign nationality, or deprivation by the government.

topics.title: Article 19: the six freedoms and the eight grounds for restricting them
topics.hook: Six freedoms for citizens only, each with its own list of reasonable restrictions, and one clause added in 1951 because the courts had struck down press censorship.
topics.story:
Article 19(1) gives **citizens** six freedoms: **(a)** speech and expression, **(b)** assembly peaceably and without arms, **(c)** association or unions, **(d)** movement throughout India, **(e)** residence and settlement in any part of India, and **(g)** practice of any profession or trade. Clause (f), the right to acquire and dispose of property, was deleted by the **44th Amendment in 1978**. The lettering therefore skips from (e) to (g), which is a favourite trick question. Because these are citizens' rights, a company or a foreign national cannot claim them, though the Supreme Court has allowed shareholders to assert them where a company's rights are affected.

Each freedom carries its own restriction clause. For **speech**, Article 19(2) lists **eight grounds**: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, and incitement to an offence. Three of these, *sovereignty and integrity*, *friendly relations with foreign States* and *public order*, were added by the **First Amendment in 1951** after *Romesh Thappar* and *Brij Bhushan* had struck down press restrictions for want of a public order ground. Restrictions must be **reasonable** and imposed **by law**, so an executive order alone will not do.

What Article 19(1)(a) has been held to include: the **right to know** and to receive information, the basis of the RTI Act; **freedom of the press**, which is not separately mentioned, established in *Romesh Thappar* (1950) and *Bennett Coleman* (1973); the **right to fly the national flag** (*Union of India v. Naveen Jindal*, 2004); the **right to silence** and not to be compelled to sing the anthem (*Bijoe Emmanuel*, 1986); and the **right to vote NOTA** as an expression of choice (*PUCL*, 2013).

**Shreya Singhal (2015)** struck down **section 66A of the IT Act** for vagueness and overbreadth, holding that a restriction must have a proximate connection with public order, not a remote one, and distinguishing discussion and advocacy, which are protected, from incitement, which is not. *Anuradha Bhasin* (2020) held that internet access is protected under 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) and that indefinite suspension orders must be published and reviewed. *Kedar Nath Singh* (1962) read sedition down to incitement to violence; section 124A has since been replaced by section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

topics.title: Elections: the Commission, the law and the reforms that came from court
topics.hook: A constitutional body with three members, a code of conduct with no statutory force that everyone obeys anyway, and a string of reforms the Supreme Court ordered rather than Parliament passing.
topics.story:
**Article 324** vests superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, the Presidency and the Vice Presidency in the **Election Commission of India**. It was a single-member body until October 1989, briefly, and permanently three-member from **1 October 1993**. The **Chief Election Commissioner** can be removed only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge; the other two commissioners can be removed on the CEC's recommendation, an asymmetry the Court flagged in *Anoop Baranwal* (2023) when it directed that appointments be made on the advice of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice, until Parliament legislated. Parliament then passed the **Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act 2023**, replacing the Chief Justice with a Union Cabinet Minister.

**Statutes.** The **Representation of the People Act 1950** deals with the allocation of seats and electoral rolls; the **Representation of the People Act 1951** deals with the conduct of elections, qualifications, disqualifications and corrupt practices. Note which Act does what, because that is the question.

**Disqualification.** Under section 8 of the 1951 Act, conviction for certain offences disqualifies a member. *Lily Thomas v. Union of India* (2013) struck down section 8(4), which had allowed a convicted legislator to continue in office while an appeal was pending, so disqualification is now immediate on conviction with a sentence of two years or more.

**Court-driven reforms.** *Union of India v. ADR* (2002) and *PUCL* (2003) established that voters have a right to know candidates' criminal records, assets and educational qualifications, giving us the **affidavit** filed with nominations. *PUCL* (2013) created **NOTA**. *Subramanian Swamy* (2013) and the VVPAT litigation led to **voter-verifiable paper audit trails**, with slips from five polling stations per assembly segment counted since 2019. In February 2024 the Supreme Court struck down the **electoral bonds scheme** as unconstitutional for violating the right to information under Article 19(1)(a).

**Model Code of Conduct.** Not a statute. It takes effect from the announcement of the schedule and lasts until results are declared, and its force is convention plus the Commission's power under Article 324.

passages.title: Basic structure
passages.passage:
In 1973 a thirteen-judge bench of the Supreme Court, the largest ever assembled in India, decided a case brought by the head of a mutt in Kerala who was challenging state land reform legislation. The dispute over his property produced almost nothing of lasting importance. The dispute over Parliament's power produced the doctrine that has shaped Indian constitutional law ever since.

The question was whether the amending power under Article 368 has limits. Six years earlier, an eleven-judge bench had held that Fundamental Rights could not be abridged by amendment at all. Parliament had answered with an amendment declaring that nothing in Article 368 was subject to the ordinary restrictions on legislation. The 1973 bench split narrowly. It overruled the earlier absolute prohibition, accepting that Fundamental Rights could be amended, but held that Parliament cannot alter the identity of the Constitution itself. Certain features, the majority said, form its basic structure and lie beyond amendment.

The judges did not agree on what those features were and deliberately declined to draw up a list. Later benches have added to it case by case, holding that judicial review, secularism, federalism, free and fair elections and the independence of the judiciary each qualify. In 1980 the Court used the doctrine to strike down two clauses that Parliament had inserted precisely to shield amendments from review, holding that limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure and that a power to destroy cannot be derived from a power to amend.

Critics have argued from the beginning that the doctrine has no textual basis and hands unelected judges a veto over the elected legislature. Its defenders point out that in the two years after the judgment, an emergency was declared, elections were postponed and a constitutional amendment placed the Prime Minister's own election beyond the reach of any court. That amendment was struck down using the doctrine.

questions.q: Which case is being described in the first two paragraphs?
options: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
questions.explain: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, decided by a 13-judge bench and arising from a challenge by the head of the Edneer Mutt to Kerala land reform laws. Golaknath is the eleven-judge bench referred to as deciding six years earlier.

questions.q: The passage refers to an eleven-judge bench that had earlier held Fundamental Rights could not be abridged. That was:
questions.explain: Golaknath (1967) held by 6-5 that Parliament had no power to abridge Fundamental Rights. Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh had earlier held the opposite; Berubari was about the Preamble and ceding territory.

questions.q: The 1980 judgment mentioned in the fourth paragraph struck down clauses of which article?
questions.explain: Minerva Mills struck down clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, which had tried to make amendments immune from judicial review. It also read down Article 31C, but the clauses named in the passage are those of Article 368.

questions.q: Which of the following has NOT been held to be part of the basic structure?
questions.explain: The right to property was removed as a Fundamental Right by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and now sits in Article 300A as an ordinary constitutional right. The other three have all been held to be basic features.

questions.q: The constitutional amendment referred to in the final paragraph, which placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny, was the:
questions.explain: Clause 4 of the 39th Amendment (1975) removed disputes about the election of the Prime Minister and Speaker from judicial scrutiny. It was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the first use of the basic structure doctrine to void an amendment.

passages.title: The five writs
passages.passage:
The Constitution gives the Supreme Court and the High Courts the power to issue five writs, all of them inherited from English law where they were issued by the Court of King's Bench. The powers are not identical. The Supreme Court's authority is itself listed among the Fundamental Rights, and can be invoked only where a Fundamental Right is at stake. The High Courts' authority sits elsewhere in the Constitution, is available for the enforcement of any legal right, and is therefore wider in subject matter, though confined to the territory over which the court has jurisdiction. One is a right the court cannot refuse to entertain; the other is a discretionary power a court may decline to exercise.

Each writ answers a different problem. One is directed at a person or authority detaining another, and requires the detained person to be produced before the court; unusually, it runs against private individuals as well as the state. One commands a public authority to perform a duty it is legally bound to perform, and is unavailable where the duty is discretionary, contractual, or owed by a private person. Two of them concern courts and tribunals rather than officials: one is issued while proceedings are still pending, to stop a body from exceeding its jurisdiction, while the other is issued after an order has been passed, to quash it. The fifth asks a person occupying a public office to show the authority by which they hold it, and may be sought by any interested person rather than only by someone personally aggrieved.

The wide reach of the first of these has made it central to Indian civil liberties. In 1976, however, a majority of the Supreme Court held that during a proclaimed emergency, no person had any locus standi to move a writ petition for release from unlawful detention. A single judge dissented, and was passed over for the Chief Justiceship as a result. The reasoning of the majority was formally repudiated four decades later.

questions.q: The writ described as running against private individuals as well as the state is:
questions.explain: Habeas corpus, literally "you may have the body", is available against unlawful detention by private persons as well as by public authorities. Mandamus is expressly not available against private individuals.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches the two writs concerning courts and tribunals?
options: Prohibition is curative; certiorari is preventive
Prohibition is preventive; certiorari is curative
Both are issued only after final orders
questions.explain: Prohibition is issued while proceedings are pending, to prevent a body exceeding its jurisdiction. Certiorari is issued after an order has been passed, to quash it. The passage describes them in that order.

questions.q: The article giving the High Courts their writ power is:
questions.explain: Article 226. Article 32 is the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction and a Fundamental Right; Article 136 is special leave to appeal; Article 142 is the power to do complete justice.

questions.q: The 1976 judgment referred to in the final paragraph is:
options: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kharak Singh v. State of UP
questions.explain: ADM Jabalpur, the Habeas Corpus case. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented and was superseded for the Chief Justiceship. The majority reasoning was repudiated in Puttaswamy (2017).

questions.q: Which statement about the two writ jurisdictions is correct on the passage?
options: Both may be refused at the court’s discretion
The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction is wider in subject matter
A High Court may decline to exercise its writ power, the Supreme Court may not refuse a petition under its own
Neither is available against a tribunal
questions.explain: The passage says one is a right the court cannot refuse to entertain and the other a discretionary power a court may decline. Article 226 is wider in subject matter, not Article 32.

passages.title: President’s Rule
passages.passage:
The Constitution provides for three kinds of emergency, and they are not equally used. One responds to war, external aggression or armed rebellion, and has been proclaimed three times, most recently and most controversially in 1975. One deals with a threat to the financial stability or credit of the country, and has never been proclaimed at all. The third, which applies to a single state rather than the whole country, has been invoked more than a hundred times.

That third power rests on the President's satisfaction that the government of a state cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, a satisfaction usually formed on a report from the state's Governor. For decades it was treated as effectively unreviewable, on the reasoning that satisfaction is subjective and that political judgments are not for courts. Governments of every party used it to dismiss administrations they disliked, sometimes within weeks of an election.

A nine-judge bench changed that in 1994. It held that the proclamation is open to judicial review, though the court would examine only whether relevant material existed and not the sufficiency of that material. More importantly, it held that the question whether a ministry retains a majority is to be settled on the floor of the House and nowhere else, least of all in the Governor's assessment. And it held that a proclamation struck down may be followed by the revival of a dissolved assembly, so that dissolution before parliamentary approval is not a fait accompli.

The same judgment made a second, unrelated holding that has been cited far more often. Dealing with dismissals of state governments accused of failing to protect secular values, it held that secularism forms part of the Constitution's basic structure, so a state government acting against it may properly be dismissed.

questions.q: The power described from the second paragraph onwards is contained in:
questions.explain: Article 356, President’s Rule. Article 352 is national emergency, Article 360 financial emergency, and Article 365 is the companion provision on failure to comply with a Union direction.

questions.q: The emergency that has never been proclaimed is the one dealing with:
questions.explain: Financial Emergency under Article 360 has never been declared. National emergency has been declared three times and President’s Rule over a hundred.

questions.q: The 1994 judgment is:
questions.explain: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, decided by nine judges in 1994.

questions.q: On the passage, how is a ministry’s majority to be tested?
options: On the floor of the House
By the President on the Union Cabinet’s advice
questions.explain: The judgment held the floor of the House is the only forum for testing majority, displacing reliance on a Governor’s subjective view.

questions.q: The maximum period for which President’s Rule may ordinarily continue is:
questions.explain: Three years, with parliamentary approval every six months. The initial approval must come within two months of the proclamation.

passages.title: The money bill route
passages.passage:
Of the two Houses of the Indian Parliament, only one may originate a particular category of legislation, and the other may not amend it. That House may accept or reject the second chamber's recommendations as it pleases, and if the second chamber does not return the bill within fourteen days it is deemed to have been passed by both. There is consequently no possibility of deadlock and no provision for a joint sitting.

Whether a bill belongs to that category is certified by the presiding officer of the originating House, and the Constitution states that his decision on the point is final. The category is defined by an exhaustive list: a bill qualifies only if it contains provisions dealing solely with matters such as the imposition or regulation of a tax, borrowing by the government, the custody of the consolidated or contingency funds, or the appropriation of money out of the consolidated fund. A bill that touches other matters as well is a financial bill of a different kind, which the second chamber may amend in the ordinary way.

The distinction has become politically significant. A government facing an unfavourable arithmetic in the second chamber has an obvious incentive to route contested legislation through the protected category. Two major statutes were enacted this way within the space of two years, one establishing a biometric identity system and another amending the law on tribunals through the annual finance legislation. Challenges to both reached the Supreme Court. In the first, a majority upheld the certification while one judge dissented in strong terms, describing the use of the route as a fraud on the Constitution. In the second, a larger bench referred the whole question of whether such certification is reviewable at all to a still larger bench, where it remains.

questions.q: The category of legislation described is:
questions.explain: A money bill under Article 110, which can only originate in the Lok Sabha and which the Rajya Sabha may only recommend upon.

questions.q: The presiding officer whose certificate is final is the:
questions.explain: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies a bill as a money bill, and Article 110(3) makes the certificate final.

questions.q: The period within which the second chamber must return the bill is:
questions.explain: Fourteen days, after which the bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Lok Sabha passed it.

questions.q: The judge who described the use of the route as a fraud on the Constitution dissented in the case concerning:
questions.explain: Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented in the Aadhaar judgment of 2018, where the majority upheld certification of the Aadhaar Act as a money bill.

questions.q: Why is there no joint sitting for this category of bill?
options: Because the Constitution forbids joint sittings entirely
Because deadlock cannot arise, the second chamber having no power to block
Because the President must assent within fourteen days
Because such bills need ratification by the states
questions.explain: The Rajya Sabha can only recommend and cannot reject or amend, so no deadlock is possible and Article 108 has nothing to resolve.

passages.title: The part that cannot be enforced
passages.passage:
One part of the Constitution confers rights that a citizen may take straight to the highest court. The next part sets out instructions to the state that no court may enforce at all, and says in terms that they are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and that it shall be the duty of the state to apply them in making laws. The framers borrowed the device from the Irish constitution of 1937, which had borrowed the idea from Spain.

The instructions cover a wide field: a social order in which justice informs all institutions; adequate means of livelihood; a distribution of material resources that best serves the common good; equal pay for equal work; the health and strength of workers; free and compulsory education for children, which was later lifted out of this part and written into the enforceable one; village panchayats; a living wage; participation of workers in management; a uniform civil code; separation of the judiciary from the executive; protection of monuments; protection of the environment and of forests and wildlife, added in 1976 along with a direction that legal aid be provided and a new instruction on equal justice.

The relationship between the two parts has been fought over for fifty years. An early view held that fundamental rights must prevail wherever the two conflict. A later amendment tried to give a class of these instructions blanket immunity from challenge under the equality and freedom articles, and the court struck that down, holding that the balance between the two parts was itself part of the Constitution's basic structure and that giving one absolute primacy would destroy it. What survives is a narrower immunity, and a practice of reading the instructions into the rights to give them content.

questions.q: The part described in the second sentence is:
questions.explain: Part IV, the Directive Principles of State Policy.

questions.q: The provision declaring them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance is:
questions.explain: Article 37.

questions.q: The device was borrowed from the constitution of:
questions.explain: Ireland, whose 1937 constitution contains directive principles of social policy.

questions.q: The instruction on free and compulsory education was later moved into:
questions.explain: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

questions.q: The judgment holding that the balance between the two parts is part of the basic structure is:
questions.explain: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down the blanket immunity given by the 42nd Amendment.

passages.title: The body that runs the largest election
passages.passage:
The Constitution gives the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament and the state legislatures, and of the offices of President and Vice President, to a single commission, and says nothing about how many people should sit on it. For most of its existence it had one. Two additional posts were created briefly in 1989, abolished, and recreated in 1993; the arrangement was challenged and upheld, and the body has been three-member since, deciding by majority.

Removal is where the asymmetry lies. The Chief Election Commissioner may be removed only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a judge of the Supreme Court, which means an address by both Houses with a special majority. The other commissioners may be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Chief, which is a considerably weaker protection and has been criticised on the ground that a majority-deciding body whose minority members serve at the pleasure of the chairman is not really a collegiate body. Appointment was for seventy years made by the government alone. The Supreme Court intervened in 2023 and prescribed a panel of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice until Parliament legislated; Parliament legislated the following year and replaced the Chief Justice with a Union minister.

The commission's most-used instrument has no statutory force at all. The code of conduct that governs campaign behaviour from the announcement of a schedule to the declaration of results is an agreement among parties, enforced by moral authority, adverse publicity, and the commission's power to censure or to bar a campaigner for a period. Its provisions on government advertising, new schemes and the use of official machinery are the ones most often invoked.

The commission also decides disputes over party symbols under a 1968 order, recognises parties as national or state based on vote share and seats, and reports to the President on the disqualification of sitting legislators on certain grounds, where its opinion is binding.

questions.q: The commission derives its powers from:
questions.explain: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission.

questions.q: The Chief Election Commissioner may be removed:
options: In the same manner as a Supreme Court judge
By a simple majority in the Lok Sabha
questions.explain: The same procedure and grounds as for a Supreme Court judge.

questions.q: Other Election Commissioners may be removed:
options: By the President on the Chief Election Commissioner's recommendation
questions.explain: Which is the asymmetry the passage identifies.

questions.q: The Model Code of Conduct:
options: Is part of the Representation of the People Act
Was inserted by a constitutional amendment
questions.explain: It is an agreement among parties, enforced by the commission's moral and residual authority.

questions.q: On the passage, the 2024 law differed from the Court's 2023 formula by:
options: Adding the Leader of the Opposition
Replacing the Chief Justice with a Union minister
Making the appointment subject to parliamentary approval
questions.explain: Parliament substituted a Cabinet minister for the Chief Justice on the selection panel.
